records.content_text:
A fraction means a part of a whole. One way to write a fraction is to write one whole number on top of another whole number with a dividing line between them. For example, $\frac{2}{10}$ means two parts of a whole that is divided in ten.
The name of the top number is the numerator, and the name of the bottom number is the denominator: $\dfrac{\text{numerator}}{\text{denominator}}$

A **decimal fraction** is a way to write a fraction using the base ten number system. Instead of writing one number on top of another, we write only the numerator after a decimal point. For example, the decimal fraction 0.2 means the numerator is 2 and the denominator is 10, so we may write it as $\frac{2}{10}$.

records.content_text:
For decimal fractions, the place values we work with are $\frac{1}{10}, \frac{1}{100}, \frac{1}{1,000}$ and $\frac{1}{10,000}$. They are called **tenths**, **hundredths**, **thousandths** and **ten thousandths**.

These place values are represented from biggest to smallest, moving to the right after the decimal point:

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
  \hline
    \text{units} & \text{.} & \text{tenths} & \text{hundredths} & \text{thousandths} & \text{ten thousandths} \\
    (1) & \text{.} & \left( \frac{1}{10} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{100} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{1,000} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{10,000} \right) \\
    \text{u} & \text{.} & \text{t} & \text{h} & \text{th} & \text{tth} \\
    \hline
    \end{array}
$$

The fractions for these place values are written in this way:

- 0.1 means zero units and one $\frac{1}{10}$
- 0.01 means zero units, zero tenths and one $\frac{1}{100}$
- 0.001 means zero units, zero tenths, zero hundredths and one $\frac{1}{1,000}$
- 0.0001 means zero units, zero tenths, zero hundredths, zero thousandths and one $\frac{1}{10,000}$.

As for whole numbers, we move to a new place value each time we reach 10. For example, this block of squares is divided into 100 parts.

One hundredth, which is $\frac{1}{100}$, may be shown like this:

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-01-001.png)

Four parts of this block of 100 squares, which is $4\times \frac{1}{100}= \frac{4}{100}$, may be shown like this:

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-01-002.png)

Ten parts of $\frac{1}{100}$, in other words, $10\times\frac{1}{100}$, may be shown like this:

![](https://electricbookworks.github.io/siyavula-open-textbooks-images/items/images/web/ebw-jss1-01-003.png)

There are 10 vertical columns in the block of squares. If 1 column out of 10 is shown in colour, we can write this as $\frac{1}{10}$. Therefore, 10 parts of $\frac{1}{100}$ is the same as $\frac{1}{10}$.

Similarly:

- 10 parts of $\frac{1}{1,000}$ is the same as $\frac{1}{100}$
- 10 parts of $\frac{1}{10,000}$ is the same as $\frac{1}{1,000}$.

In this notation, the numerator is written after a decimal point and the denominator is not written down. heading_path.h3: Worked example 4.6: Converting decimal fractions to common fractions

records.evidence_quote: Write 4.08 as a common fraction.
records.answer_text:
Step 1: Use the number of digits after the decimal point to determine which power of ten is the denominator.

There are 2 digits after the decimal point. Therefore, the denominator is:

$$
\frac{\phantom{00}}{10\times10}=\frac{\phantom{00}}{100}
$$

Step 2: Starting from the first non-zero digit of the decimal fraction, write the digits without the decimal point. This becomes the numerator of the common fraction.

$$
\frac{408}{100}
$$

Step 3: Find the simplest form of the fraction obtained in Step 2.

$$
\frac{408\div4}{100\div4}=\frac{102}{25}
$$

placement.rationale: This exposition directly teaches the first conversion method for this AO: convert common fractions with power-of-ten denominators to decimals using place value.

records.evidence_quote: When a common fraction has a denominator that is a power of ten, it is easy to convert it to a decimal fraction. You dealt with the place values of decimal fractions in Chapter 1. $$ \begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{units} & \text{.} & \text{tenths} & \text{hundredths} & \text{thousandths} & \text{ten thousand
records.content_text:
When a common fraction has a denominator that is a power of ten, it is easy to convert it to a decimal fraction. You dealt with the place values of decimal fractions in Chapter 1.

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
  \hline
    \text{units} & \text{.} & \text{tenths} & \text{hundredths} & \text{thousandths} & \text{ten thousandths} \\
    (1) & \text{.} & \left( \frac{1}{10} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{100} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{1,000} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{10,000} \right) \\
    \text{u} & \text{.} & \text{t} & \text{h} & \text{th} & \text{tth} \\
    \hline
    \end{array}
$$

Consider the fraction $\frac{30}{1,000}$. If the denominator is 1,000, the corresponding decimal fraction must have 3 digits after the decimal point. We may write it in a place value table.

$$
\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
  \hline
    (1) & \text{.} & \left( \frac{1}{10} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{100} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{1,000} \right) & \left( \frac{1}{10,000} \right) \\
    \text{u} & \text{.} & \text{t} & \text{h} & \text{th} & \text{tth} \\
    \hline
    0 & \text{.} & 0 & 3 & 0 &  \\
    \hline
    \end{array}
$$

The place value table shows that we have zero units, zero tenths, three hundredths and zero thousandths. Remember that we do not write zeros at the end of decimal fraction. This fraction is therefore written as 0.03.

Similarly, the common fraction $\frac{30}{100}$ may be expressed as 0.30, which is written as 0.3. The common fraction $\frac{30}{10}$ may be expressed as 3.0, which is written as 3.

heading_path.h3: Worked example 4.7: Converting common fractions to decimal fractions

records.evidence_quote: Write $\frac{5}{6}$ as a decimal fraction.
records.answer_text:
Step 1: Divide the denominator into the numerator. If it cannot divide, write a zero.

$$
\require{enclose}
\begin{array}{r}
0\\
6 \enclose{longdiv}{5}\\
\end{array}
$$

Step 2: Put a decimal point after the zero and after the numerator.

$$
\require{enclose}
\begin{array}{r}
0.\\
6 \enclose{longdiv}{5.}\\
\end{array}
$$

Step 3: Add zeros after the decimal point in the numerator.

$$
\require{enclose}
\begin{array}{r}
0.\phantom{0000}\\
6 \enclose{longdiv}{5.0000}\\
\end{array}
$$

The numbers 5; 5.0; 5.00; 5.000; 5.0000 and so on all represent the value 5.

Step 4: Carry on with the division.

$$
\require{enclose}
\begin{array}{l}
\phantom{00} 0.8\,3\,3\, ...\\
6 \enclose{longdiv}{5.0\,0\,0\,0}\\
\,\underline{-0}\downarrow\,\downarrow\,\downarrow \,\downarrow \\
\phantom{00} 5\,0 \\
\,\underline{-4\,8} \\
\,\phantom{000} 2\,0  \\
\phantom{00}\underline{-1\,8} \\
\phantom{00000} 2\,0   \\
\;\phantom{000}\underline{-1\,8}  \\
\;\phantom{000000} 2\,0   \\
\end{array}
$$

Step 5: Write down the answer.

The division will carry on forever, because we keep on getting the same remainder. This is called a recurring decimal. We write it with a dot above the digit that repeats.

$$
\therefore \frac{5}{6}=0.8\dot{3}
$$

records.evidence_quote: - A common fraction is written as $\frac{\text{numerator}}{\text{denominator}}$. - A proper fraction is smaller than 1, for example $\frac{2}{7}$. - A mixed number consists of a whole number and a proper fraction, for example $5\frac{1}{6}$. - An improper fraction is larger than 1, for example $\frac{9}{4}$. - Equivale
records.content_text:
- A common fraction is written as $\frac{\text{numerator}}{\text{denominator}}$.
- A proper fraction is smaller than 1, for example $\frac{2}{7}$.
- A mixed number consists of a whole number and a proper fraction, for example $5\frac{1}{6}$.
- An improper fraction is larger than 1, for example $\frac{9}{4}$.
- Equivalent fractions have different numerators and denominators but the same value, for example $\frac{1}{2}=\frac{2}{4}=\frac{4}{8}$.
- A fraction is in its simplest form when the numerator and denominator have no common factor.
- To compare fractions, we must express them with the same denominators. The lowest common denominator is the smallest whole number into which all the denominators can divide without a remainder.
- A decimal fraction is written in decimal notation, where the numerator is written after a decimal point and the denominator is a power of ten.
- In decimal notation, the decimal point separates whole numbers from fractions.
- If there are three digits after the decimal point, the denominator is $10\times10\times10=1,000$.
- A percentage is a fraction with denominator 100, written with only the numerator followed by a percentage symbol.
